newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq, U.N. agree to defer missile engine issue.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, U.N. agree to defer missile engine issue.

text.p: Iraq and the United Nations have agreed to put off a dispute over removing scrapped missile engines until February next year, chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus said on Wednesday.
"We have agreed to freeze it (the missile problem) temporarily until our next meeting in February," he said.
Iraq last month prevented a team of U.N. arms inspectors from moving the engines outside the country for analysis. Ekeus said the file on banned long-range missles still remained open.
Asked how many more banned missiles the United Nations thought lraq was still hiding, he told reporters: "It is a significant number that is not accounted for."

Ekeus has previously said that between six and 16 missiles were unaccounted for. He said Iraq's refusal to allow his team to remove the scrapped missile parts to determine their origin was a serious breach of a key U.N. Security Council resolution.

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction has information about the number of Scud missiles that Iraq acquired from the Soviet Union before the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis. It later discovered that Iraq was capable of producing its own missiles.

Ekeus said both sides had agreed to continue discussions on the missile issue early next year. Removal of the overall curbs on Iraqi oil exports depends on testimony from Ekeus that Iraq has complied with disarmament demands.

Ekeus said that at this stage it was impossible to give Iraq the certificate. Iraq said on Tuesday it resumed partial oil exports of $2 billion in line with a U.N. offer designed to alleviate the suffering of the Iraqi people under crippling U.N. trade sanctions, imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
